## Shuldroon

Shuldroon was a War Wizard of Cormyr in the late 15 century DR.

Personality
Per Storm Silverhand's intelligence, Shuldroon was zealous and overconfident, a killer, and was out to make his mark. Internally, he was arrogant, and believed in the superiority of War Wizard command over knights. He sneered a lot.

Abilities
Shuldroon could feel large amounts of magic being unwound, and he could wield wands. He also knew more than one offensive spell.

Possessions
Shuldroon carried a wand of lightning bolts or similar.

Relationships
During his last mission, Shuldroon was part of a team together with Rondrand and Athlar; all squads were under the command of Kelgantor. Storm Silverhand considered Hondryn one of his flunkies.

History
Shuldroon was a part of the squad sent to capture Elminster Aumar at Tethgard after he stole the Royal Gorget of Battle from the Royal Palace of Suzail. While approaching Elminster's refuge, his team broke formation out of unfamiliarity with the terrain. He provided some unprompted advice in the aftermath, right before they noticed the ripples in the Weave from Elminster destroying an enchanted item, and were precipitated into action.

During their meeting with Elminster, Shuldroon ran his mouth quite freely, gloating and boasting, and even issued commands that were ignored by the rest of the team, though Kelgantor did not contest them. He continued to gab until Elminster admitted the gorget was no more, at which point, Shuldroon immediately attacked with his strongest spell, which, combined with everyone else's spells, blew up Tethgard, slaying Kelgantor on the process. He was unmoved by the deadly counterattack of the Simbul, instead employing his wand to fire off a lightning bolt; it slew a highknight. His next discharge was somehow augmented and rebounded by an unknown spell of Elminster's; it went right back to his wand, which exploded, killing him.

## Shadowroot

Shadowroot sacs were small, faintly glowing, bulbous fungus growths found in the Shadow-cursed Lands surrounding Moonrise Towers in the Western Heartlands in the late 14 and 15 centuries DR.

Usages

Despite their overwhelmingly putrid stench, shadowroot sacs were harvested for their alchemical properties. The sacs and their secretions were refined into a vitriol that possessed a peculiar effect on those who smelled it. This vitriol had a smell of cloying sweetness but provoked bile rising in one's throat. The same smell seemingly sharpened the senses of those who smelled it.

Shadowroot vitriol could be combined with certain types of ashes to brew elixirs of viciousness.

## Shadow crossing (Evernight)

The shadow crossing in Neverdeath graveyard was a portal allowing for passage from Neverwinter in the Material Plane to Evernight in the Shadowfell. As of the late 15 century DR, it was under the control of Valindra Shadowmantle and her Thayan forces.

Description
The portal made use of circle magic and was activated by sprinkling a special powder into an eternal flame that burned within the Neverdeath cemetery. A nearby teleportation circle granted easy access to the crossing for Valindra Shadowmantle and her apprentices.

Unlike the many so-called Crevices of Dusk that connected Neverwinter and Evernight, this portal was not a naturally occurring gap in reality, but rather a purposefully opened shadow crossing that had been established at a weak point in the veil between the planes.

Geography
In Neverdeath, the crossing was located at the center of the graveyard in a section known as Craftsman's Rest.

In Evernight, users of the crossing appeared between a pair of iron gates that otherwise appeared to lead nowhere. This site was located atop a small hill in a mostly abandoned neighborhood to the south. It lay within sight of the Thayan headquarters.

Defenses
On the Evernight side of the crossing, hidden Thayan guards kept watch over the portal. These included undead who were loyal to Valindra rather than to the city's ghoul rulers.

History
As of, Valindra Shadowmantle and her Thayan forces were making use of the shadow crossing to prosecute their evil plans in Neverwinter, to establish a foothold in Evernight, and to secure access to the Shadowfell Road. Wanting to keep her out of the Shadowfell, her Netherese enemies sought to disrupt her access to the crossing. To avoid alerting Neverwinter to their presence, the Netherese aimed to use indirect means to thwart her, such as by hiring adventurers.

## Shadow crossing

A shadow crossing, sometimes called a shadow portal or a Bleak Path, was a location where the boundary between the Shadowfell and the Prime Material plane was so thin that it was possible to travel between the two planes. Some shadow crossings occurred naturally whereas others were portals that had been intentionally created.

Description
Shadow crossings oozed with darkness, cold, and gloom. They varied in size from small fissures in reality that were too small for travel to entire areas the size of a cemetery. A shadow crossing could appear as a blot of deep darkness, a passage into utter blackness, or as a normal place with no indication that it led to somewhere else. They were often hidden or concealed within areas of deep darkness, but in some cases, it was possible to stumble through one on accident. They could sometimes be spotted by the way that light would quickly fade as it passed through (although other shadow crossings were disabled by light). Individuals with darkvision noted how their sight could simply end at the crossing's threshold.

Some crossings were known to people who lived near them—whether because they had been intentionally created or because local superstitions spoke of them—and such sites might be adorned with crude shrines to gods and demon lords of death. Some rifts were too small to recognize, but might become the source of terrifying urban myths stemming from Shadowfell denizens stalking and snatching unsuspecting victims through them.

Location
Naturally occurring crossings might arise due to a planar conjunction or disaster, or could manifest in a few types of locations: low-lying areas that were nearly always kept in deep shadows (such as in the Underdark, caverns, the bottoms of ravines, dark forests, foggy swamps, or abandoned buildings), places where spirits or the dead were prevalent (such as cemeteries, crypts, or open graves), or locations where much death had occurred (such as battlefields or sites of mass killings). Naturally occurring shadow portals were a known hazard for travelers in the Lowerdark, where entire tunnels would be blocked by permanent gateways into the plane of shadow. These began to appear about  below the surface, and became more prevalent as one traveled deeper and deeper.

Even artificial portals were often erected in places where the stench of death was pervasive because the veil between planes was more easily breached in such areas.

Within the Shadowfell itself, mortal inhabitants often lived near a reliable shadow crossing.

Activation
Most shadow crossings were not continually active, and instead required some condition to be met in order to open them. This might include only opening on certain occasions—such as specific times of day, special days out of the year, or when a new moon or an eclipse was observed—while others might require special keys or commands—such as the hand of someone recently slain or a special magic powder. A shadow crossing might only function if in complete darkness, and would close if exposed to light. It was said that circle magic could be used to create or open a shadow crossing, and any inactive crossing could be opened with the Shadow Passage ritual.

While some crossings were bi-directional, others were one-way trips into the Shadowfell. It was estimated that about 1 in 5 of the naturally occurring portals in the Underdark were one-way only.

Notable Shadow Crossings
 Citadel Umbra on Gwynneth in the Moonshae Isles was permeated with crossings to the Shadowfell and to the Feywild.
 Krystel Mansion in Battledale was a shadow crossing such that the entire estate overlapped into the Shadowfell.
 An open grave at Chalet Brantifax.
 A shadow crossing was created in Neverwinter's Neverdeath Graveyard that led to the Shadowfell city of Evernight.
 The Shadow Veil was a massive rift between the planes that bisected and gave name to the town of Veil in Thay.
 The archmage Keraptis, while he was in the process of creating a permanent shadow crossing by binding himself to the Shadowfell, created a temporary shadow crossing in White Plume Mountain whilst it was relocated to Toril.

History
Shadovar strike teams and their agents were known to make use of shadow crossings to launch attacks into enemy territory, such as in Cormyr.

In the late 15 century DR, agents of Thay identified a route that connected their realm all the way to the Sword Coast North that relied on a series of steps back-and-forth between the treacherous Shadowfell and remote parts of the Prime Material plane. They called this the Shadowfell Road.

The city of Neverwinter was known to contain many small breaches into the Shadowfell—known as "Crevices of Dusk"—through which the undead inhabitants of Evernight would hunt. Banderhobbs were likewise known to grab their prey through small fissures between the planes, and in fact had an innate ability to detect shadow crossings and to sense potential prey on the other side of them.

Scarecrows were said to be more powerful if created on or near a shadow crossing.

## Shadowfell Road

The Shadowfell Road was a disorienting route that connected the city of Evernight to the nation of Thay through the Shadowfell. It was discovered and used in the 15 century DR by agents of Thay loyal to Valindra Shadowmantle and Szass Tam to further their clandestine schemes in the Sword Coast North.

Description
Travel along the Shadowfell Road was grueling and filled with horrors, but thanks to the space-warping properties of the Shadowfell, it was a quick but complex route across Faerûn. The magic of the route was such that the "road" only really existed if approached and followed precisely, making it easy to get lost without following a Thayan caravan. The route's true secrets were known only to a few.

Some stretches of the road were treacherous, following mountain ledges, crossing rickety wooden bridges, or passing through haunted terrain. Certain parts were particularly difficult to navigate with carts, if not impossible.

Geography
Unlike a mundane trail, the Shadowfell Road comprised many disconnected paths—sperated by many miles if not across planes—that were linked by subtle teleportation effects that had to be activated by following the route precisely. Efforts to take shortcuts or to join the path midway, or any failure to take the correct turn or to go through a specific archway or cave would mean backtracking to fix the mistake.

The route began in the Shadowfell city of Evernight. It exited the city via the southwestern gate before turning east through the Burning Woods, where extreme heat, pervasive smoke, piles of ash, and raining fire were potentially fatal obstacles. The trail passed nearby to where the Dread Ring was located on the Material Plane, which connected to the Shadowfell Road via a portal (although the Dread Ring itself was not technically on the Road). The route then proceeded into the darker and more confusing depths of the Shadowfell for a few hours before arriving at its first teleportation point, which led to the haunted labyrinth known as Endless Alleys. The Alleys were not navigable by cart, and so the Thayans were known to leave carts at both this entrance and the exit further along the route (sometimes defended by their undead minions).

As the Shadowfell Road continued, it jumped back-and-forth between different places both within the Shadowfell and across the Material Plane. It ran through a wide array of regions and landscapes, including graveyards, mountains, ruins, swamps, and villages (some abandoned and others populated). One stretch bounced through secluded passes, vales, and ledges in the mountain ranges of central Faerûn before reentering the Shadowfell in a cave. Some of the locations through which the Road passed on Toril were not physically located between its starting point near Neverwinter and its endpoint in Thay.

The Road eventually terminated in the town of Veil in western Thay, a village split by a permanent rift between the planes that left half of it inside the Shadowfell. However, the Thayans who used the route would proceed through Veil and along a winding trail on the Material Plane that led to Surcross, their final destination. This path was well defended: it was trapped with concealed necromantic glyphs that psychically assaulted any living creature that passed over them, and the road was lined with impaled corpses that would rise to attack Thay's enemies.

History
The Thayans gained control over the Shadowfell Road sometime shortly before . This entailed not only discovering the very precise series of twists and turns required to traverse the whole route, but also subjugating the various peoples and monsters along the route who would threaten their caravans and bribing the ghouls and vampires of Evernight with food (in the form of both living and deceased humanoids) for access to the route's western end. They used the Road to move supplies and troops to and from the Dread Ring and Surcross, and to move bodies to the Dread Ring from Neverwinter's Neverdeath graveyard (which was linked to Evernight via a shadow crossing).

As a military supply route, the Shadowfell Road became a major point of tension between Thay and Netheril, and as the Shadovar–Thay War intensified, the Netherese sent their flying fortress-city Kolthunral to attack Surcross and deny the Thayans access to the Road. However, they were unable to do so decisively as of 1479 DR because the Shadow Veil in Veil disrupted their fortress's meteor tubes, which worked by routing projectiles through the Shadowfell to generate momentum. Meanwhile in Evernight, the two sides were forced by the ruling ghouls to keep their war out of sight, which the Thayans were content to do as long as they continued to receive supplies along the Shadowfell Road.

Notable Locations
 Evernight, the western terminus of the Road.
 Endless Alleys, a haunted labyrinth of alleyways and rooftops.
 Still Waters, an inhabited but intensely haunted swamp.
 The Obsidian Ziggurat, a looming pyramid amid an abandoned village.
 Village of the Mad Druid, a town where all of the people pretended to be undead.
 Veil, the eastern terminus of the Road, from which it was a short journey to Surcross.

Inhabitants
Unless accompanying a Thayan caravan or otherwise travelling in large numbers, monsters and factions along the Shadowfell Road were liable to attack any travelers. The Thayans themselves were a threat, as were their Netherese rivals for control of the Road. In addition, dark ones, nightmares, shadows, and undead monsters were potential threats, as were bandits and gangs of lost wanderers. Travelers near Evernight might be attacked and robbed by the Glumguts (a clan of dark creepers in service to the Netherese) who lurked along the Road, or by the fiery undead and animate ash trees of the Burning Woods. Meanwhile, travelers approaching Veil had to contend with the Thayan garrison who defended the Shadow Veil, which included both living and undead soldiers in fortified bunkers equipped with arcane siege engines.

Some of the villages through which the Road passed were populated with shadowborn inhabitants who simply wished for travelers to leave them alone, while other sites were abandoned and haunted by incorporeal spirits.

## Shadowborn

Shadowborn referred to any mortal person or creature who was native to the Shadowfell. It was understood that such individuals' souls were connected to that plane.

Description
In many cases, shadowborn mortals were indistinguishable from mortals who had been born and raised on the Material Plane, and could live for generations in the Shadowfell without undergoing any physical or mental changes, although their shadows might appear darker or deeper. In other cases, the gloom seemed to seep into them. Shadows appeared to dance in their eyes and they looked almost deathly: their features were hollow or sunken, their skin was paler or darker than natural, and occasionally their bodies degenerated or seemed to waiver as if insubstantial. Mentally, some shadowborn individuals might exhibit melancholy, madness, paranoia, or nervousness, and might become unable to distinguish between good and evil.

While the term "shadowborn" generally referred to mortal inhabitants of the Shadowfell, it could also be applied to those whose souls had become tethered to that plane in some other fashion, such as by being born near a shadow crossing or having been touched by a creature of shadow (such as a wraith or specter). The descendants of shadowborn individuals might also inherit shadowborn traits even if born outside the Shadowfell. Normal mortals could also undergo a dark and forbidden ritual to draw the power of the Shadowfell into themselves, becoming a being known as a shadowborn stalker. Shadar-kai were considered shadowborn.

Abilities
Shadowborn felt empowered both physically and mentally when in darkness. Some shadowborn were further able to use their souls as conduits to the Shadowfell, allowing them to channel the powers of shadow and death. This could grant them a wide range of abilities, such as the power to summon darkness, conceal themselves in shadow, empower their attacks, teleport short distances, create body doubles, or manifest tendrils of darkness.

Culture

Shadowborn maintained settlements and even kingdoms within the Shadowfell, often making their homes not far from a shadow crossing or in places that had long ago been secured by explorers or previous inhabitants. Whether human, elf, halfling, or something else, such settlements tended to be outwardly very normal, with the shadowborn raising families, engaging in business and trade, setting out on adventures, and offering safe haven to travelers. However, nearly all such settlements concealed some dark secret or unique curse which trapped or troubled its inhabitants (in addition to the strain of fending off the horrors and cultists who also dwelt in the Shadowfell).

They were said to practice the ancient art of shadowdancing.

Outlook
Shadowborn had a tendency toward dour worldviews and grumpy or sullen personalities. Mood swings were seen as normal, and they might come across as morose and negative, especially in the eyes of more lighthearted folk. When interacting with others, they might stare blankly, speak darkly, or react slowly. Outsiders tended to be somewhat off-put by how calm and accepting shadowborn tended to be in the face of death, which many shadowborn came to regard with a sense of bleak inevitability after having lived in the Shadowfell.

Relationships
Shadowborn tended to regard the various cultists of the Shadowfell with suspicion or hostility, and considered the worship of Orcus to be a crime.

It was said that cobalt dragons who dwelt in the Shadowfell preferred to dominate tribes of shadowborn humanoids when they needed servants. Death giants were said to subjugate shadowborn trolls and ogres.

History
The original Shadovar of Thultanthar were shadowborn, and their descendants inherited some connection to shadow.

As of the late 15 century DR, Still Waters was inhabited by shadowborn of various races who dwelt in stilted huts above the haunted waters. At that same time, the so-called Village of the Mad Druid was inhabited by shadowborn who pretended to be undead. The city of Gloomwrought was home to shadowborn.

## Shadowborn stalker

A shadowborn stalker was a humanoid who had undergone a radical transformation into a creature suffused with the power of the Shadowfell.

Description
The transformation turned the humanoid's skin to a pale gray, their hair to pure black, and their eyes to pupil-less white. The power of the Shadowfell embedded itself into both their body and soul, and created a sinister aura of shadow around them.

Abilities
Shadowborn stalkers gained darkvision as well as the abilities to turn invisible or to create a  zone of magical darkness for a few seconds whenever they wished.

Society
Becoming a shadowborn stalker required striking a bargain with the powers of the Shadowfell to access the forbidden lore and dark rituals that enabled the transformation. The most likely individuals to pursue this path included assassins, thieves, and warlocks—especially among goblins, drow, and shadar-kai—who favored stealthy approaches to their problems.

Notable Shadowborn Stalkers
 Wei Chiang, a merchant and drug smuggler active in Westgate in the late 15 century DR.

## Ship (longship)

The Ship was the longship of the hill giant Huzza, a pirate of sorts who roamed about the Inner Sea in the 14 century DR.

Description
With a crew of 70 untrained goblins, the Ship was slow and ungainly in the water. Huzza caught other ships by throwing crew goblins at the rigging, occasionally landing a hit and allowing the goblin to sabotage the lines. With the target slowed, Huzza and the Ship could catch up, loot the target vessel, and eat the crew.

History
Huzza obtained the Ship when its crew landed near his home and attacked him, only to be eaten to the last member. He found some gold in the longship and decided to use it to find more gold and food on the sea, and so crewed it with his goblin servants and set off. He recruited several more goblin tribes to work aboard his vessel, but his use of them as ammunition steadily depleted their numbers and only his immense strength and size kept them from mutiny or desertion.

## Shalanka

Shalanka was an eladrin twilight incanter who served as the protector of the so-called Village of the Mad Druid in the Shadowfell as of the late 15 century DR.

Personality
She was insane and delusional, and as a result, not very perceptive. Living in the Shadowfell had twisted her mind such that she believed living creatures to be abominations and that undead were natural and normal. However, her grasp on reality was tenuous enough that although she believed herself to be the guardian of a village of undead, the inhabitants were in fact living people who merely pretended to be undead to placate her and earn her protection.

Abilities
She used her powers to manipulate a battle, teleporting herself and her foes or binding and blinding her enemies, all to gain advantage for herself and her minions.

Activities
She patrolled the Shadowfell Road just outside the Village of the Mad Druid, attacking and seeking to slay any living travelers with her pack of undead animals.

History
Although she was dangerous and unstable, Shalanka was appreciated as the defender of the Village of the Mad Druid, and the citizens tried not to upset her as they knew that they would be condemned to death without her.

As of, Shalanka had come to realize that she was not strong enough to contest either the Thayans who had pacified the Shadowfell Road nor their Netherese rivals, thus she did not attack agents of either realm.

## Shadow Veil

The Shadow Veil was a sizable and permanent planar rift in Thay that allowed for crossing between the Material Plane and the Shadowfell.

Description
The Veil appeared as a tall, shifting curtain that looked like a combination of a shadow and a heat mirage. Anything seem through the Veil appeared dim, flickering, and almost unreal.

The presence of the Veil both empowered and interfered with portals to and from the Shadowfell.

Geography
The Shadow Veil cut through the town of Veil—where it provided access to and from the Shadowfell Road—and across the surrounding landscape. This region was often darkened by the shadow of the looming cliffs of the Thayan Plateau and the smoke of eruptions from the Thaymount.

History
During the mid-to-late 15 century DR, Thayans led by Valindra Shadowmantle made use of the Shadow Veil when mastering the Shadowfell Road in pursuit of their goals at the Dread Ring near Neverwinter. Thayan guards and fortifications were placed on both sides of the Veil to defend access to the Road.

In the, the Netherese flying city of Kolthunral arrived in the area to besiege Surcross and Veil and to deny the Thayans access to the Shadowfell Road. The city remained close to the Veil in order to ensure that its portals functioned correctly, however the fluctuating planar energies of the Veil also interferes with the city's mighty meteor tubes—which worked by hurtling projectiles in and out of the Shadowfell—by causing their missiles to miss their targets. Thus, the areas beneath the Veil were protected from the Netherese bombardment that decimated the nearby Charnel Fields.

By that same time, a Thayan commander and Banite priest named Renault Abrecht believed that he had devised a means to collapse the Shadow Veil.

## Shrine of the Sheaf

The Shrine of the Sheaf, later renamed Fox Tower, was a former keep turned into a shrine to Chauntea and later commandeered by bandits in the the mid–8 century DR.

The Shrine lay across Buckralam's Starn from the road that led into it.

Structure
The place was a former keep. It had a courtyard.

Interior
The feast hall was lit by candle wheels, and had a minstrels' gallery up top. Bedchambers lay beyond the hall, which also connected to the kitchen. Another passage led to the back of the keep, the pantries, and to Beldrun's Room, which had once been the abode of a priest and since been converted into furniture storage during the takeover by the Iron Fox. In the, the Iron Fox's forces were broken and decimated by the combined efforts of the Chosen of Mystra Elminster Aumar and a local woman, Immeira. Nevertheless, it remained known as Fox Tower until at least .

## Sharindala

Sharindala was an undead sorceress in Ripplestones during the 8 century DR.

Description
While an undead, Sharindala was mostly grey and brown bones, with some long brown hair still attached to the remains of her scalp.

Relationships
She knew Caladaster Daermree while he was but a boy.

Abilities
She had strong wards around Scorchstone Hall, almost certainly of her own making. She was later able to use her spells to regain more of a semblance of life.

Possessions
She wielded at least one wand that fired volleys of magic missiles, likely a wand of missiles. One of the spells she gained afterwards granted her the power to speak, despite being reduced to bones.

History
Sharindala became undead somehow and then her home burned down; due to the strong wards, no one approached.This occurred when Caladaster was just a boy; he recalled the incident when he was an old man in 767 DR, suggesting it was in the late 600s or early 700s DR.

In the, a wandering Elminster Aumar entered her home to cache away magic so that others might find it; he then came across her animated skeleton, cowering in a closet. Though she attacked him to no effect with her wand, Elminster was not furious or offended. After she refused his offer to help her find lasting rest, he offered her new magic instead, giving her a spellbook; one of the spells allowed a caster with no throat to speak, even speak magic words. He also bid her use that magic to beseech Mystra over the spellbook when she had the time.

She later did beseech Mystra, who put some meat on her bones, just enough for her to be able to weep. After Caladaster Daermree, and the wandering scholars Tabarast and Beldrune returned from Karsus' Keep, she showed herself at the local tavern, the Fair Maid. Her magic had returned her to flesh everywhere above the hips, though she was still far from being able to eat or drink. She asked Beldrune for one of the dressing gowns he brought from Karsus' Keep, but Caladaster gave her the robe he was wearing. They left the place to go for a walk, with Sharindala insisting they had much to talk about, and told all in the tavern that all that had been said of the god Azuth was true.

## Shimmering

Shimmering was a unique enchanted quarterstaff with a spearhead on one end, that was hidden within the Haunted Halls of Eveningstar in Cormyr in the 15 century DR.

Powers
A staff made out of steel, Shimmering possessed a giant bane enchantment that made the weapon deadly to giants, dealing additional damage to these creatures, and making strikes extremely hard to avoid. Additionally, Shimmering dealt radiant damage with each attack.

History
Sometime long before the 15 century DR, a giant was killed by Shimmering deep within the Haunted Halls. The giant's body was pinned to the ground with the weapon and eventually, time ravaged the giant's body to be nothing more than a massive armored skeleton. As of the 15 century DR, the Fallen Giant was still in the dungeon. Anyone who were to remove Shimmering from the skeletal undead would end up awakening the angry undead giant.

## Shade (disambiguation)

Shade could refer to several concepts, many of which related to the Shadovar people who were brought to Faerûn during the Return:This does mean that as of 1372 DR, "the shadowy shade shadows, Shadow's shades, and shade shades of Shade (overshadowed by the Princes of Shade) shadowed the shade hunters in the shadow of Shade from the shadows" was a grammatically correct and contextually plausible phrase that one could say.

 The Netherese enclave of Thultanthar, also known as Shade or the City of Shade,
 The Empire of Shade, the greater holdings of Thultanthar once it conquered parts of Faerûn,
 the Princes of Shade, the ruling family of the domain, made up of Telamont Tanthul and his sons,
 shades, shadowstuff-infused mortals who comprised the elite of Thultanthar's empire,
 the general population of Thultanthar's empire such as the Shadovar, shadar-kai, and krinth, simply called shades as a whole as well, and
 shade hunters, treasure hunters who specialized in looting Netherese ruins from underneath the shades of Thultanthar.

Other uses of shade related more broadly to shadow magic and living shadows:
 The Shade's Veil, an ancient Imaskari artifact,
 Shadevar, ancient shadowy beings present at the dawn of creation,
 the Shade Lord, a powerful living shadow,
 various creatures related to living shadows in general, such as shade wolves,
 shades, an illusion spell created by Lord Shadow that produced quasi-real imitation conjurations,
 create shade, a Zakharan spell that produced a patch of comfortable shadow,
 mirror shades, a kind of spectral undead that lurked in mirrors,
 Aurgloroasa, a shadow dragon also known as the Sibilant Shade, and
 King Kymer of Tethyr, known as the Shade King for his mundane skulduggery.

## Sharran hideout (Storm Horns)

A secret Sharran hideout was hidden in the foothills of the Cormyrean Storm Horns, home to many Sharrans and the infamous Dedryk Black.

Description

The approach to the hideout was prepared with tree-blocked paths, traps, and groups of Sharran defenders. Inside, the cave was partially fitted with furnishings, with various gates and traps installed to slow down intruders. It was also fitted with two altars to Shar, with a particularly large cavern serving as the main shrine and focus for their operations.

Geography
The hideout was located some distance east of the Starwater River, in the forested lower foothills of the northern Storm Horns.

History

The caves were used by the Wheloon escapee Dedryk Black, who had gathered up a sizable cult of Sharrans that he treated as his flock. Their existence was discovered when a group of Cormyrean hunters stumbled across the cultists in the woods, who fled in a panic and dropped their holy symbols of Shar. This drew the interest of the Magistrates Abella Toth, Celia Pendrick, and Barthold Moncrief in Eveningstar, who investigated from there. Abella Toth in particular hired adventurers who had traveled from Eberron to search the area, and after some intense fighting Dedryk and his closest followers had been captured and prepared for transportation back to Wheloon.

Inhabitants

The caves and surrounding hills were home to wild wolves and mountain lions. To support their defenses, Dedryk Black's followers summoned air and ice mephits to fight alongside them, and kept caged wolves as guard dogs. The Sharrans also kept a large owlbear penned up in the hopes of using it as a weapon, though it proved to have no loyalty for them, only hunger.

## Shaloss Ethenfrost

Shaloss Ethenfrost was a wizard of Silverymoon. Once the Captain of the city's Spellguard, he proclaimed himself High Mage, ruling the city for only two months whilst under siege by the Black Horde.

Personality
Shaloss was already a Captain in the fledgling Spellguard by 1235 DR, but, nonetheless, he craved more. So great were his desires, his greediness, that he took up the empty mantle of High Mage for himself, hoping its added duties (and the power that came with it) would satisfy him. When Alustriel Silverhand arrived in Silverymoon, saving "his" city in the process, Shaloss also revealed a calculating side of his. He knew that she would quickly gain public support, and so suddenly engaged her in magical combat to eliminate her as a future political rival.

Relationships
Despite being their High Mage, Shaloss's relationship with the Silvaeren was tenuous at best, for their concerns about the orc siege far outweighed any worries they might have had about the wizard's tyrannical behavior. The man did, however, have a pair of apprentices. These two, at least, were willing to fight alongside him against the usurping Alustriel.

History
At some point between Eleint of  and 1235 DR, Shaloss was made a Captain of the Spellguard, which was a project of Silverymoon's last officially elected leader, Silvermayor Theomel Scalson. It was during that latter year that the military's leader, Warlord Khallos Shieldsunder, took control of the city, whose army Shaloss and the other Spellguards fought alongside to repel the Black Horde.

In one battle, however, Khallos, too, was slain. The city's forces rallied together for another month as more and more orcs arrived to besiege Silverymoon's walls. It was then that Shaloss took the name of High Mage for himself, foregoing any formal process of election, and he was able to keep the title for two months as the city continued to eke out its own survival. Despite his time on the Silver Throne and unlike previous High Mages, he never made for himself a library and study in the dungeons of the High Palace. In fact, he never found out that these existed at all.

By the end of Shallos's two months, however, help arrived. Alustriel Silverhand, aided by her sister, Storm Silverhand, and the unified forces of the Harpers, finally ended the siege that had threatened the Gem of the North for so long. Though the woman seemed a ray of hope to the Silvaeren, Alustriel threatened the weak tyranny Shaloss had put in place, and so, moving quickly once she passed into Silverymoon's walls, he and his apprentices attacked her with the full force of their Art. It was a spectacular combat, but even outnumbering her three-to-one, both Shaloss and his aides were utterly destroyed.

## Shadovar invasion of Wheloon

The Shadovar invasion of Wheloon was a brief conflict fought inside the Wheloon Prison in the mid-1480s DR, which involved the forces of Thultanthar infiltrating the prison and attacking the defending Cormyrean garrison. A key part of the invasion was the Shadovar's use of the Abyssal Planus Mechanus Nether Scroll to open a passage called the Shadowfell Nexus through the Shadowfell that they used to secretly bring troops and supplies into the city. The conflict between realms naturally affected the prisoners who lived there as well, including the Wheloon natives.

History
Goals

The conspiracy inside the Wheloon Prison was intended to recruit the entire population of prisoners to the Netherese cause, drive the Cormyrean forces from the city, and use it as a base from which to attack Cormyr itself, all while using the Shadowfell Nexus to move in and out of the fortified prison unopposed. This was ultimately designed to provide a distraction from the Cormyrean front with Sembia, where much of their forces were already focused, and allow the real invasion to strike from that direction when the Purple Dragons and War Wizards were drawn away. A third strike would come from the newly-created glacier enclave of Archwizard Amskar, bearing an army of orcs, giants, and other auxiliaries.

Shadovar Infiltration

By the understanding of the Cormyrean garrison, the population of the prison was simply made up of the Sharran prisoners (those proven to be, or suspected) and the non-Sharran prisoners (typically violent and hardened criminals), who were a threat to each other but not their captors. Patrols of Purple Dragons and magistrates were able to enter the city at will and perform their duties without particular danger, but the secret arrival of the Shadovar and their allies quickly overturned the status quo. Entire patrols of soldiers began to go missing, lone survivors would emerge with cursed wounds and damaged minds, and Oldstone Hall could be seen from over the walls pulsing with a strange magical energy.

The prisoners became far more active as well, with most of the Sharrans quickly joining up with the Netherese forces, and there was nothing preventing the most violent convicted criminals like Zastra from carving out territories at the expense of everyone else. Groups of Purple Dragons, War Wizards, and magistrates were isolated and picked off at the hands of enraged prisoners who had lost their fear and sensed an opportunity to escape. The lesser-known Wheloon natives remained essentially neutral and uninvolved in the fighting whenever possible, as they were hard-pressed simply surviving as the situation deteriorated. They remained fortified within Harvest House and the drainage culverts, under attack from violent gangs.

This early period of secrecy lasted a few weeks, with the Netherese forces hidden behind the rioting prisoners. However, during this time the headstrong adventurer Oriphaun Huntsilver smuggled his way into the prison, chasing rumors of lost relics that he could add to his collection. Although he entered the city selfishly, he quickly discovered that it was no ordinary riot and found the Netherese forces within. Knowing that this posed a grave threat to the kingdom, he pursued an investigation into the shadowy conspirators, eventually uncovering their plans while remaining undetected.

One of the earliest signs that something was wrong had been when the prominent Sharran prisoner Dedryk Black somehow vanished from the prison, only to be rediscovered in the foothills of the Storm Horns while leading a cult. Unbeknownst to the jailors, Dedryk had used the Shadowfell Nexus to simply walk out of the prison. Though Magistrate Abella Toth had managed to capture him, Barthold Moncrief's group was attacked while returning the prisoner a short distance from Wheloon. The raid led by the lizardfolk shaman Srass Marnanr sought to rescue Dedryk Black on behalf of Netheril, though it was ultimately unsuccessful and Dedryk was returned to Wheloon.

On arrival in Wheloon he was taken to the Magistrate's Office for interrogation by Cornelius Latrimor, only for the Shadowfell Nexus to briefly and violently overlap with the docks, depositing a small army of living shadows and enraged prisoners amidst the shocked Cormyrean forces. Though they were warded off, the distraction allowed the assassin Teralyn to slay the Magistrate and send Dedryk and other Sharran prisoners to freedom through the Shadowfell.

Once they were securely established, the Netherese forces were mainly based in northern Wheloon around Oldstone Hall, home of Archwizard Tyrvus, his Nether Scroll, and the Shadowfell Nexus, and the Netherese recruiting center, a fortified building where General Marthir took in and trained prisoners. More Netherese forces were scattered about the surrounding area, including the merchant's townhouse where the shadar-kai Karleth held his twisted court, the Netherese tavern where the invaders could go to relax, the abandoned bookstore, and the aptly-named Shar Manor.

Cormyrean Counterattack

At the prompting of the Amaunatori priest Dai Rolno, Knight Faline Abbot sent adventurers to investigate the circumstances of the Wheloon natives in the drainage culverts, who were being assaulted by a large gang led by the Troise siblings. In the process of the grim underground fighting, Porto, Aramiya, and finally Athea Troise were slain, destroying not just the family but the gang itself. The action also led to some cooperation between the Wheloon natives and the Cormyrean forces, who began to acknowledge that many of the prisoners trapped in the city had been innocent of any Sharran worship.

Following that, Wizard of War spymaster Gaspry Bennik acted on reports that an unknown figure was organizing and unifying all the prisoners into a single massive gang. To investigate the situation he sent in a team of infiltrators led by Fordwin, supported by adventurers, to pose as criminals and join the group. On reaching the target, however, the Cormyrean team was captured by the Sharran priest Stanwicke Gall and his assistant Tulla Chymbal, who had been unifying and proselytizing the disparate prisoners. The adventurers managed to fight their way out of the ambush and confront Stanwicke, refused his offer of a job with Netheril, and cut him and Tulla down. In addition to saving the captured Cormyrean agents, this prevented the Netherese from easily recruiting the prisoners that weren't already Sharrans.

Following that, a rescue mission was launched by Knight Hargrove Jalt into the heart of Netherese territory in order to save the magistrates Aloysius Cornwall and Fledren Hull, who had been captured by the shadar-kai commander Karleth. The heroes of Cormyr attacked his base at the old merchant's townhouse that he had fitted with cages, and fought through his shadar-kai and howler forces to save the magistrates. In the end, Karleth fell along with his champions Yzthmeth and Kuttar, and the magistrates were saved from his cruel executions.

With a better understanding of the situation, Swordcaptain Iden Krell sent a group to infiltrate and destroy the Netherese recruitment center. Within, Wheloon prisoners were recruited with promises of glory, revenge, and freedom, and converted to the worship of Shar. With hard fighting the Cormyreans defeated the underofficers Darobard and Rantha, and gained access to the central tower where General Marthir waited. Although he summoned a fearsome nightcrawler from the Shadowfell, Marthir fell as well, ruining the Netherese attempts at recruitment and disrupting their command structure.

The adventurous Oriphaun had completed his own investigations, and had determined that the Netherese had used a Nether Scroll to create the Shadow Nexus. Knowing that the situation was well above his capabilities, he dropped a letter explaining all he had learned with the Cormyrean garrison, asking for assistance. Willing to take the chance, Wizard of War Jacinta Last sent a team into Oldstone Hall itself to meet Oriphaun and find and capture the Nether Scroll. While Oriphaun climbed up the side of the tower in an attempt to sneak in and abscond with the Scroll, the others entered by force, using Mirrors of Shadows to step between the material and shadow worlds and bypass the Netherese defenses. While Oriphaun was actually successful in entering the tower from a window and laid hands on the Nether Scroll, he was immediately caught by Archwizard Tyrvus and magically paralyzed. The Cormyrean team arrived soon after and joined battle with the Archwizard, who used the Shadowfell Nexus itself as a weapon against them, though to no avail. The arcanist was eventually overcome and fell in battle, and the Nexus ceased with his death. Oriphaun recovered quickly from his incapacitation and after a brief thanks and farewell disappeared with the Nether Scroll in order to keep it out of Netherese hands permanently.

Aftermath
As a result of the failed invasion, much of the Netherese forces were destroyed along with their commanding shades Marthir and Tyrvus, and without the Shadowfell Nexus the remaining soldiers and local recruits remained trapped inside the prison. The most irreplaceable loss was that of the Nether Scroll, which was carried off by Oriphaun Huntsilver and protected by the Harpers. Although the Netherese pursued in force and briefly recaptured the artifact, they ultimately failed to recover it.

The failure of the Wheloon Shadowfell conspiracy and the loss of the Nether Scroll was followed by the destruction of Archwizard Amskar's newly-raised enclave in the Storm Horns and its mythallar (also thanks to Oriphaun). These setbacks meant that the subsequent Shadovar invasion of Cormyr of 1486 DR under Lady Marsheena was severely blunted and eventually failed by the end of that year.

Combatants

Archwizard Tyvrus maintained supreme command of the operation, though his attention was split with maintaining the Shadowfell Nexus, so General Marthir was thus responsible for much of daily command. Beneath them, a number of shades held power, including Lord Monte, Auralace, and Trassex, the strangely masochistic Karleth held much influence over the shadar-kai forces including Nichts Volpe, the Mistress of the Hounds, and priests such as Stanwicke Gall and Sombra proselytized among the masses. They brought in large numbers of shadar-kai fighters, with Sharran priests and arcanists providing magical support. Their forces were supplemented by large numbers of prisoners, initially those who were already Sharrans but then expanding to the general population, many of which had more than enough reasons to fight against Cormyr. They also used shadows, gargoyles, and other creatures like howlers to supplement their forces.

Cormyrean forces were largely made up of of Purple Dragons under the command of Oversword Edric Crastmere and Constal Davny Selkin, supported by War Wizards and priests from the church of Amaunator. They were aided by specialists like Gira Falantine, on Shar, Waric Altamor, regarding the Netherese Empire, Kalo Mandanas, on the Shadowfell, and Jacinta Last, who was an expert on the Nether Scrolls., allowing the defenders to better understand the situation and develop a counter-attack. They were willing to accept the aid of adventurers in investigating the interior, including renegade shadar-kai, over-enthusastic Amaunatori priests, and disgraced Purple Dragons.

The ongoing connection to the Shadowfell also allowed other shadowy creatures like nightcrawlers and eyes of shadow to enter the material realm and interfere, though Archwizard Tyvrus believed them to be a negligible threat to the operation. Opportunistic night hags were among these interlopers, and many were hired by the Netherese as mercenaries (with significant reservations).

The lizardfolk who lived around and beneath Wheloon had initially been hired by Cormyr to act as a second line of defense and block escapes, especially through the drainage culverts. As the invasion proceeded, some were subverted to the side of the Netherese through extravagant payments, while others like Snake and Salak remained sensibly uninvolved.

The mail was mostly black and bore a large white skull design on the chest.

Though a fairly large suit of mail, it was specially designed by the eladrin to be lighter and not impede spellcasting. It also carried powerful enhancements to certain destructive elemental styles of magic, making it ideal for a flashy spellcaster.

The armor was in the 'possession' (sans wearer) of the giant spider Greenstalker, who had laired near Granwell Keep in the King's Forest. It may have been found by Harpers looking for the Abyssal Planus Mechanus Nether Scroll held by the Shadovar arcanists in the Keep.

## Shilku Bay

Shilku Bay was a coastal inlet located along the western side of Chult. It was one of the few places suitable for landing a ship along the Wild Coast.

Description
An active volcano sat to the west of the bay. This volcano erupted during the 15 century DR, creating a river of lava that perpetually flowed into the bay, which caused the water to hiss and turn poisonous with sulfur. Clouds of hot ash and even fiery stones falling from the sky made any effort to land on the western shore by ship exceedingly dangerous. However, the eastern shore continued to have safe landing places.

History
During the heyday of Hrakhamar, trade roads connected it to Shilku Bay.

The eruption of the nearby volcano was still ongoing as of the time of the death curse in the late 15 century DR. During this time, Liara Portyr—leader of the Flaming Fist at Fort Beluarian—sought to fund an expedition of adventurers to scout Shilku Bay and determine if it was worthwhile to establish an outpost there.

Notable Locations
 Shilku: This town sat on the western edge of the bay.

## Shondrin's Packsack of Plenty

Shondrin's Packsack of Plenty, or simply The Sack, was a general store in the settlement of Bargewright Inn in the Savage Frontier in the mid-to-late 14 century DR. It was run by Shondrin.

Location
It stood in the upper part of Bargewright Inn, on the northern side of the road known as the Rise, between Belvyn's House of Good Cheer and Ruldarr's Pipes, Locks, Tobacco, and Fine Furniture.

Services
Small and jam-packed, the shop sold all sorts of things, including dry goods and an assortment of practical supplies, like candles, rope, and outerwear clothing. Prices were slightly above the average market price and Shondrin occasionally accepted items in trade, which he sold in the store. Hence, it included some secondhand items such as hardware and old armor and weaponry. If Shondrin didn't have what a customer wanted in stock, he could tell them the nearest place they could find it.

While Shondrin rarely dealt in enchanted items, they did turn up from time to time, apparently misidentified. Volothamp Geddarm once discovered a bag of holding shaped to resemble a statuette of a fat dragon, the head of which swung back to reveal the opening; it was later sold. There were also tales of travelers purchasing a seemingly mundane old sword, only to find it enchanted and possessing unexpected powers.

## Shondrin

Shondrin was a retired sailor of the Sword Coast and the proprietor of Shondrin's Packsack of Plenty in the settlement of Bargewright Inn in the Savage Frontier in the mid-to-late 14 century DR.

Description
He was a fat and jovial fellow, and full of wild stories from his seafaring days.

Activities
From "the Pack", Shondrin sold all sorts of things, including dry goods and an assortment of practical supplies, like candles, rope, and outerwear clothing. Shondrin occasionally accepted items in trade, which he sold in the store. Hence, it included some secondhand items such as hardware and old armor and weaponry and even magical items, though Shondrin rarely dealt in them knowingly. If Shondrin didn't have what a customer wanted in stock, he could tell them the nearest place they could find it, which might be as far as Waterdeep, Athkatla, or even Calimport. While this wasn't always helpful, it was a point of pride to Shondrin that he had complete, up-to-date knowledge of all legal, open-market vendors.

His house stood at the very center of the settlement, between the Rise and the Back streets and next door to Rinthar's house.

Location

The floating leaky inn collected payments before the stay but asked no questions of its guests, whether guests brought swords, chained up captives, or came prepared for a brawl. ## Sharess' Caress

Sharess' Caress was a festhall located on Wyrm's Crossing in the Outer City of Baldur's Gate in the late 15 century DR.

Location
Sharess' Caress stood on the eastern side of Wyrm's Crossing – the bridge that connected Rivington and the Twin Songs neighborhoods of the Outer City, just past the checkpoint gate that allowed entrance to the bridge, across the street from Fraygo's Flophouse.

Structure
The festhall was a structure of three stories and one sub-level. It opened into a thin taproom filled with seats at the bar, the hostess counter, and several booths. The taproom had one stair up to the second and third floors and two stairs to the sub-level – the kitchen and its large larder to the left from the entrance and a curtained entertainment chamber with a stage and musical instruments. The second and third floors had more seating and tables available for the guests, and the third floor expanded across the bridge to the western side and housed several thematic lodgings where guests met similarly thematic escorts.

The second entrance into the festhall was accessible from the bridge's walkways that overlooked the cliffs and the River Chionthar on the opposite side of the building. The walkway had several tables available to customers who preferred fresh river air to perfumes and incense of Sharess.

The "Nymph's Grotto" room was decorated in a sylvan manner and had a sizable bath. "Elminster's Library" was styled after a wizard's lair. The "Underdark Pleasures" room was quite self-explanatory. And lastly, "Devil's Den" was a lavish and splendorous room fit to satisfy some of the most posh devils.

History
During the Absolute crisis of the, Mamzell Amira, the festhall's proprietress, sought investigators who would be interested in seeking out the coinlass named Ffion Goldgrind, better known as the "Stern Librarian," who disappeared and left her clients' bookings unattended. Ffion fell victim to the Murder Tribunal cultists of Bhaal, and her body was discovered next door at Fraygo's Flophouse. During the same time, one special consort took residence in the festhall's "Devil's Den." This suave individual was Raphael, who used the room to forge infernal contracts rather than offering sexual favors.

Notable Inhabitants

Employees
 Amira, the festhall's over in the late 15 century DR and the owner of especially vain cat named Kira.
Ffion Goldgrind, the dwarvish coinlass who entertained guests of "Elminster's Library."
Hoots Hooligan, a big and intimidating bartender. Her self-made drink – Hoots' Hooch, was a potent mixture that possessed some peculiar effects on the imbibers.
Naoise Nallinto, the coinlass calling herself a "nymph," who entertained guests of the "Nymph's Grotto."
 Sorn Orlith and Nym Orlith, drow twins who worked as expensive companions and escorts, servicing clients together. The twins laying together was harmless, according to them, as Sorn was magically rendered sterile.
Sauceman Chorizo, the festhall's dwarvish cook.

Customers
Arfur Gregorio, a toymaker from Rivington who found himself involved with the Cult of the Absolute's terrorist acts.
Earspoon and Borgus Elamin, a duo of shady associates of the Gate's infamous Guild.
Kith'rak Voss, a one-time customer who fraternized with devil Raphael but declined the contract.
Korrilla, Raphael's servant and aide, who was often found partaking in Hoots's offerings while her boss was in his room upstairs.
Valeria, a callus hollyphant investigator for the Flaming Fists of the Gate.

## Shadowsponge

Shadowsponges, also known as air stealers, were notorious gargantuan sponge-like, air soaking creatures that inhabited the void of Wildspace.

Description
These sponge-like creatures had gray, rubbery ovoid bodies, consisting of many branched air-sacs that protruded off of a central mass. These sacs were all studded with a multitude of patches that acted as sensory points, allowing them to see and "smell" air from up to a distance of  with the void of Wildspace. Their bodies were quite gargantuan in size, measuring up to  in length on average, though they were also known to grow beyond that.

Behavior
These creatures exhibited a semi-intellect, though when gathered together into a group their minds worked together on a high intellectual level. They never fought amongst themselves or collided with one another. They primarily focused their day to day lives around continuously absorbing air from atmospheres, though would the large, stable atmospheres of planets.

Abilities
They were vulnerable to electrical and fire-based attacks, though were impervious to harm from mere heat and would instead recover from high degrees of heat. When harmed by either electricity or fire, their bodies would expunge a thick, noxious cloud of gas. This gas would foul  of air within a  spherical area, gradually turning it deadly.

Most notably, shadowsponges were capable of reattaching any severed part of their body and could even merge with the bodies of others to create a larger shadowsponge.

When gathered together into a group shadowsponges were capable of gathering electrical charges and discharging them to devastating effects, equivalent to one chain lightning spell or two lightning bolts. However, merely passing through a "charged herd" on its own posed no immediate threat.

Combat

Shadowsponges fought by ramming their gargantuan bodies into foes and enveloping them. Most shadowsponges could only envelop a single human-sized creature at a time, though larger ones were capable of enveloping two at a time. Due to their porous nature victims would not suffocate while in their embrace, though they suffer the effects of their noxious gas. Whilst enveloped by a shadowsponge it was impossible to cast spells, fight with bludgeoning weaponry, or generally use ones arms. Any attempt to attack a shadowsponge would harm the enveloped victim as well. Severe harm or outright death would cause a shadowsponge to convulsively release any creatures they have enveloped.

Ecology
These creatures could often be found moving through the void of Wildspace on their own, lacking family units. Though some small shadowsponges have been observed corralling others of their kind into groups out of instinct. These groups, referred to as "herd clouds", traveled on long voyages. Herds clouds were studied with great interest by sages in the 14 century DR.

They played no part in any food-chain and had no observable reproductive cycle.
Diet
Shadowsponges exhibited a very unique and varied form of subsistence. They derived nutrients from gas, light, electrical energy, and heat energy. However, their main source of subsistence was the nutrients they derived from air.
Usages
Throughout the ages alchemists and spell researchers across various races studied in vain to find some use for the tissues and essence of shadowsponges. Over time, some sages and alchemists began to theorize that the essence of herd clouds could be harnessed in some manner to guard against magical electric-based attacks or even generate them. However, such experiments did not draw fruitful results. Beyond their potential usage for the magical arts, it was found that the rubbery tissue of shadowsponges was inedible.

Some spacefarers, however, found ways to utilize shadowsponges as portable atmospheres for prolonged voyages or offensively as air stealers. This involved trapping them within either a spacewreck or a large, sturdy spacegoing storage container and then forcibly dragging it along with their spelljammer. Those wishing to utilize shadowsponges for the latter purpose would drag them through the atmospheres of planetoids or skim the atmospheres of worlds.

The secondary usage involved bringing them into the atmosphere of, or into a collision course with, either a planetoid, base, or spelljammer. This particular usage was known to be utilized by enemies of the Elven Imperial Navy. In both cases a shadowsponge would absorb and store any usable air, however, the shock of this treatment would ultimately cause them to gradually die and necessitate their storage vessel being cut, lest the connection poison all of the air within a spelljammer.

History
One experiment with shadowsponges involving some tinker gnome devices made to create and store energy, observed that a low-energy application of the shocking grasp spell made them release 25% of the atmosphere they had stored.

Rumors & Legends
Some sages have theorized that shadowsponges were merely a stage in the lifecycle of some advanced fungoid lifeform. According to this theory, shadowsponges entered a certain state from the absorption of nutrients derived from gas and upon doing so would seek out a planet. They would enter its atmosphere, fall to its surface, and metamorphosize into spores to begin the next stage of its lifecycle.

However, other sages, such as Elminster of Shadowdale, have cautioned that though this theory cannot be discounted outright, no substantial evidence exists for several aspects of this theory.

## Shond Tharovin

Shond Tharovin was a human wizard of the mid-to-late 14 century DR who used the Living Gem to briefly rule Schamedar in Calimshan in 1367 DR. He founded the Cult of the Living Gem and fought the Living Gem War before he was turned into an immortal gibbering mouther and exiled from Calimshan.

Possessions
For a time, Shond possessed the Tome of the Unicorn, from which he was able to summon the demilich form of Shoon VII. During the Time of Troubles, he relinquished the Tome to Shoon.

Shond's most significant and powerful possession, however, was the Living Gem. With it, he became powerful enough to take the city of Schamedar.
He used a magical mirror to scry on enemies and attack them remotely with spells stored in the Gem. He claimed that he could reach all of Faerûn through the power of the Living Gem. But Shond was driven mad by the Gem, which he believed to be alive. He called it his advisor, and claimed that he was following its desires. When he was turned into a gibbering mouther, he lost ownership of the Gem to the Cult of the Living Gem.

Shond was presumed to have a lair somewhere on the southern coast of Thordentor amongst the Nelanther Isles.

History
In the, Shond visited the island of Ruathym, and stole the Tome of the Unicorn from the Green Room library. The last page of the book had the demilich Shoon VII trapped within. Shond was able to summon Shoon from the book, and struck a bargain with him. Shond agreed to free Shoon by bringing him seven souls, in exchange for information relating to the location of the Living Gem.

In the, on the day that the Time of Troubles began, Shond had taken the Tome to the Cloud Peaks. He ambushed a caravan transporting the elf wizard Zallanora Argentresses and summoned forth Shoon. Shoon devoured the souls of the members of the caravan, but as the chaotic magic of the Time of Troubles took effect—instead of devouring Zallanora's soul, Shoon's soul switched places with hers. This left Shoon free of the Tome, in Zallanora's body—and Zallanora in the demilich body trapped in the Tome. Shond and Shoon destroyed any evidence of the caravan to cover their tracks. Now that Shoon was free, he upheld his bargain with Shond and told him the location of the Living Gem.

Shond spent the next decade following Shoon's cryptic directions: excavating a ruined temple to Ghaunadaur beneath the Forest of Mir, southwest of the Vorpal Tower.

In Mirtul of the, Shond finally claimed the Living Gem from the ruins. In Kythorn, he used the power of the Living Gem to oust all members of the ruling council of Schamedar and took the title of syl-vizar, caleph of Schamedar. He used a magic mirror together with the Gem to remotely view and attack Artouk Fanzir, one of the ousted members of the council who had escaped Schamedar. By Flamerule, he had established the Cult of the Living Gem, and began construction on a temple named the House of the Gem.

In Eleasis, Shond used the power of the gem to fight against a rebellion started by the nascent Seven Satraps, along the River of Ice. Thus began the Living Gem War. In Eleint, an archmage named Yoond Shalshymmyr defeated Shond by sacrificing his own life and cursing the tyrant into the form of a huge and immortal gibbering mouther. By Marpenoth, Shond had been forced into the sewers of Schamedar by its citizens, and the Living Gem fell into the hands of the Cult of the Living Gem. Shond eventually floated out of the city into the Shining Sea, crying for revenge as he went.

After he was forced out of Schamedar, Shond disappeared. In Nightal of 1367, a wizard named Nardulkyn claimed that Shond had gained the ability to retake the form of a human, and that he had drifted west of Calimport. Nardulkyn claimed to have invented a spell that could track Shond, but only when he took human form. His destination was much-rumored, and locations such as Tethyr, the Nelanther Isles, or Skullport were theorized.

In fact, Shond Tharovin drifted westward and washed up on the Singing Rocks, an archipelago in the Sea of Swords to Calimshan's west. He made any or all of these isles his lair by 1370 DR, an unknown but terrible threat to any sailor who might venture near those mysterious isles.

Abilities
Although once a wizard of respectable power, Shond's exposure to the Living Gem had fundamentally transformed him in unknown ways and he was cursed into the form of a gibbering mouth, so it was impossible to guess what he was capable of. However, since he had no hands, he could not cast spells with somatic component, but he had no shortage of mouths with which to speak those with verbal components.

As an enormous gibbering mouther, Shond could pull his mass together to cover more than  of one of the Singing Rocks or, by stretching his amorphous form along the seabed to up to, could extend across nearly all the northern isles. The chemicals exuded by his aberrant body also repelled most predators. He could also change shape back into a human thrice a day. Together, this gave him an unusual method of travel: stretching his gibbering mouther form to its furthest reach, changing into a human there, and snapping the rest of his body to this new location, and repeating this a few times to hop great distances; this allowed him to make quick and surprising escapes.

In any shape or size, Shond was fully aware of all parts of his mass and could speak no matter what mouth he used. The chemicals exuded by his aberrant body repelled most predators, as he appeared poisonous to eat, which aid him whilst in the water.

Activities
Those aware of Shond suspected he must still study arcane magic.

Despite his downfall, curse, and exile, Shond was patient in plotting his cruel revenge on the Cult of the Living Gem.

Relationships
Given his presence in the waters around the Singing Rocks and ability to speak, it's possible Shond had some contact with the kraken (or krakens) known as the Curse of Irphong and its armies. He was also likely familiar with the undead skeleton whales that guarded a certain underwater lair close to Thordentor, but not that it belonged to the Twisted Rune. Should it ever resurface, he would try to obtain another powerful magical relic, Kayas the Krakenscourge, in order to manipulate the Curse of Irphong and other krakens.

## Sholsarrath

Sholsarrath the Lame was a dim-witted kobold warlock of the Skulking Dragon clan who traded his own head to a demon, actually just an imp, Yargulbuzul some years before the late 14 century DR.

Description
After entering his pact, Sholsarrath was missing a finger and a foot.

History
Sholsarrath was a kobold shaman who, in order to avoid a grisly death, entered a warlock's pact with the demon Yargulbuzul, who offered him power and, subsequently, the leadership of the clan. The price was the kobold's own finger and a foot. After the said fiasco, Sholsarrath the Lame committed to taking care of his tribe and keeping it happy and well-fed – for a kobold, that meant raiding local farms. With help from the tribe's old chief, Sholsarrath trained the kobold warriors to be a fearsome force. Soon after the plunder began, the Skulking Dragons became hated and feared among the locals. The clan's infamy rose so much that a band of traveling adventurers decided to end the kobold menace.

The five adventurers rode out of the village of Houndstown and quickly were able to track the Skulking Dragon clan. The kobolds might have been a nightmare for the local peasantry, but they were naught but pests for weathered adventures, who slaughtered the clan's best warriors en masse. Desperate once again to escape sure doom, Sholsarrath the Lame evoked Yargulbuzul's name once again, demanding salvation and a way to escape. Yargulbuzul claimed that it would be a tough feat to accomplish and demanded one last payment from the kobold, a payment greater than anything he paid before. The dim-witted warlock agreed frantically to Yargulbuzul's demands – the kobold's head. When the five adventurers reached the shaman's lair, they witnessed a happy imp decapitating Sholsarrath and carrying his soul to the Abyss.

Sometime later, Sholsarrath the Lame's head was fashioned into an enchanted mask fashioned to be worn by warlocks. The Head of the Lame Kobold found its way into the hands of Dayne Lynneth, a merchant from Tyr's Eye plaza in the Blacklake District of Neverwinter in the .

## Shadow jelly

Shadow jelly was a species of carnivorous non-intelligent oozes, native to the Plane of Shadows and found lurking in the darkest corners of deepest dungeons.

Description
Shadow jellies appeared to be large, pulsating pools of living darkness. Unlike other shadow creatures, shadow jellies were tangible. Experienced adventurers had a chance of spotting a huge patch of unnatural darkness, but they were clearly visible in full light.

Abilities
They were capable climbers and possessed blindsight that allowed them to feel the prey as far as .

Combat
In battle, shadow jellies darted forward, slamming at the opponents, trying to attach to their victims and drag them into the darkness to be consumed. When a shadow jelly touched a creature, it began draining its physical strength, gradually weakening it.

Ecology
These solitary creatures were shadows driven by one thing—the constant insatiable desire to consume living things and light. When prey fell into their pseudopods, the living shadow ooze enveloped and engulfed the creature, slowly dissolving it within its digestive organs.

Shadow jellies inhabited the deepest and darkest areas on the Prime Material plane when away from their hope in the Shadowfell. They lay in wait until prey was near and then quickly transformed into fearless and tireless ravenous predators. However, most creatures who were as big as a shadow jelly or bigger, were left alone.

## Shortbow of Gesen

The Shortbow of Gesen, also known as the iron bow of Gesen, was a unique and powerful shortbow crafted by Gesen Khan, a legendary chieftain amongst the Tuigans, some time before the mid-14 century DR. It was believed that no ordinary man could bend the bow nor could survive its deadly missiles.

Description
The iron bow of Gesen was the finest bow to had ever been created by Gesen Khan. Despite its craftsmanship, it appeared to be a bow typical in appearance for such weapons crafted by the Tuigans – it was lacquered and black with a shimmering bowstring of green. The shaft was made out of iron, masterfully worked to appear almost indistinguishable from wood under casual examination. Despite that, it was light and could be drawn more effectively than iron should allow.

Powers
The shortbow's magic was fueled by the energy it drew from the planes. The bow focused the planar energy into spears of lightning and arrows of fire that were fired out instead of normal arrows. Once per day, the bow also could fire an arrow of slaying. Additionally, the iron bow of Gesen possessed potent +4 or +5 enchantments that made the weapon's damage more destructive and guided the missiles toward their targets. Its offensive magics had one side effect – they granted the wielder protection against electricity. When the wielders used ordinary or enchanted arrows with the bow, instead of bolds of electricity, the arrows jumped from the quiver onto the bow via its magic, allowing the wielder to unleash arrows four times quicker than a normal bow. Additionally, its range was double that of a normal shortbow.

Legends also stated that an arrow unleashed from the iron bow of Gesen could splinter a tree and shatter stone, and it was believed that anyone who wielded the weapon received a gift of perfect aim even after the bow left their hands.

Lastly, there were dangers in wielding this artifact. It possessed the curse that had a chance of gradually transforming the wielder into a horseman of the steppes, body and mind. The transformation gradually changed their appearance and could cause them to forget how to read or sail or some other knowledge and skills not typically known to a Tuigan warrior, instead becoming experts in bowmanship, horseback riding, etc. This transformation did not affect the individual's class, but once complete, the wielder became fully possessed by the artifact, becoming compelled to take on adventures and good deeds and causes. The curse could be lifted by returning the bow to Gesen Khan's shade somewhere in the Hordelands or by breaking the bow via 1,000 blows with the hammer of Gesen.

History
Historians stated that Khan planned to retire after selling this powerful weapon, but instead, he was cut down by a thief, who disappeared with the shortbow of Gesen. All while, legends stated that the shortbow of Gesen was interred with Gesen Khan after his death somewhere in the Hordelands' steppes, despite the weapon being seen in many other people's hands afterward. In the following years, the bow became a highly sought after artifact. Both Shadow Thieves and the Cowled Wizards of Athkatla tried to find the weapon, the Shadow Thieves – to be used for assassinations, and the Cowled Wizards – to study, the goal that was made complicated by the fact that many fake iron bow of Gesen being created.

By the, the shortbow of Gesen was somehow broken apart, its pieces scattered. The bowstring made its way into the hands of a group of mind flayers who established a hidden refuge in the sewers beneath Athkatla. The shaft was stored in the tannery and home of Rejiek Hidesman a serial killer, apprehended or killed in 1369 DR.

Once both pieces of the bow were assembled, Cromwell, a master smith of Athkatla, may have had repaired the artifact.

Description
These animals were visually similar to white stags. They had larger hoof prints than more common deer.

Abilities
This deer variant was able to teleport short distances. It was also immune to mind-affecting spells.

Combat
Shadow harts fought using their hooves and antlers. To escape mid-fight, they used their teleportation abilities.

Uses
The horns of these animals could be used to create cures for some illnesses. The heart could be used to craft a lesser amulet of health.

Ecology
These rare wild herbivores often traveled alone and used their teleportation abilities to quickly travel short distances even when not in danger.

In the, at least one shadow hart lived in the foothills connecting Hilltop and Blumberg. The hunter Ferran Valiantheart was looking to kill it to retrieve its horns to cure his wife from an unspecified disease. The deer either died or escaped based on the actions of Drogan Droganson's pupil, who either killed the deer, helped it, did not meet it, or avoided it altogether.

## Shadow body

Shadow body was a psionic power of the psychometabolism discipline that allowed psions and wilders to become their own shadow.

Effects
Through the use of this power, a psion and everything on their person would be transformed into a living shadow, unattached to anything, allowing them to blend into areas of darkness. While the power was active, the psion was capable of moving along walls, ceilings, and even liquid surfaces such as waterfalls, with the same ease as walking on solid ground. However, this power did not make one's body malleable like a shadow—they could not squeeze through any enclosed spaces they wouldn't normally be able to fit through, such as a keyhole.

Additional benefits provided by shadow body included darkvision, increased protection from most forms attack, and immunities to drowning, diseases, and poison. However, while in shadow form, a psion could still be partially harmed by all manner of acids, electricity, and fire. They also were incapable of physically manipulating or interacting with objects, though could still use their other psionic powers as normal.

Those using shadow body could be detected by any spells or psionic powers that detected thoughts, life, or presences, such as true seeing.

Displays
Manifesting this power produced a standard auditory display.

Users
Shadow body was an innate psionic ability for shadow efts.

Known/Notable Users
 Eldenser, an amethyst great wyrm.

## Sherrod Starym

Sherrod Starym was an elven wizard of Myth Drannor's House Starym who visited Eveningstar in the late 15 century DR.

Description
Sherrod had tanned skin and shoulder-length white hair swept back.

History

During the Shadovar activities after the Shadovar invasion of Wheloon, Oriphaun Huntsilver spied upon them in the Storm Horns. Archwizard Amskar captured him and took him into captivity, leading to his Harper allies throwing their efforts into tracking him down, rescuing him, and undoing the Netherese schemes.

To aid these efforts, they called in an old favor with the Myth Drannan mage Sherrod, who arrived in Eveningstar to lend his expertise. By the simple expedient of checking where he couldn't scry, he deduced that Oriphaun was exceptionally well protected and hidden inside Rungnir's glacier. The Shadovar operation was also well warded, though not even their best work could hide the growing power of their recovered mythallar. With the approval of the Harpers, Sherrod sent a team into the mountain glacier to find Oriphaun and fight the Netherese.

The grand project turned out to be an entire flying enclave, armed to wage war upon Cormyr. The Harpers managed to rescue Oriphaun, slay Archwizard Amskar, and destroy the enclave's flight pillars, sending it careening into a mountainside. Sherrod was suitably impressed by their report when they returned.
